candidate.answerReason: P must finish first, and S has at least three runners ahead of it. Each of Q, R, and T can finish third.

methods.label: Combine the finishing-order conditions
methods.explanation:
The conditions place \(P,T,Q,S\) in that order: \(P\) finishes before \(T\), \(T\) before \(Q\), and \(Q\) before \(S\). Also, \(P\) finishes before \(R\).

Consequently, \(P\) is ahead of all four other runners and must be first. The three runners \(P,T,Q\) are ahead of \(S\), so \(S\) must be fourth or fifth. Neither \(P\) nor \(S\) can be third.

To check the remaining runners, the following orders, written from first to last, satisfy every condition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P,T,Q,R,S &&\text{puts }Q\text{ third},\\
&P,T,R,Q,S &&\text{puts }R\text{ third},\\
&P,R,T,Q,S &&\text{puts }T\text{ third}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus exactly \(\boxed{P\text{ and }S}\) could not have finished third, choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: Combining before-and-after statements and exhibiting possible orders requires only elementary logical and ordinal reasoning.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task distinguishes impossible finishing positions from possible ones under finite order constraints. The method combines the constraints, eliminates P and S, and supplies a valid order for every remaining candidate. Understanding ordinal positions supports the reasoning; permutation formulas and formal truth operations are not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: The constraints give P before T before Q before S, and P before R. Thus P is first and S is fourth or fifth. The three displayed valid orders establish that Q, R, and T can each finish third.
